item.title: Kratos Phishing Kit Takedown, Chick-fil-A Credential Stuffing, and NuGet Typosquat
item.content:encoded:
Police Dismantle Kratos Phishing Kit Built to Steal Microsoft 365 Sessions and Bypass MFA — Should Read

German and US law enforcement dismantled the Kratos phishing-as-a-service infrastructure, taking over 200 servers offline and disrupting a Microsoft 365 session-theft kit used by about 1,800 customers. The kit could bypass ordinary MFA by stealing session cookies, so affected users may need session revocation and phishing-resistant sign-in, not just password resets.

  • German and US law enforcement took down the core infrastructure of the Kratos phishing kit, and Indonesian authorities arrested the man they say developed and operated it.
  • The Frankfurt public prosecutor's cybercrime unit and Germany's Federal Criminal Police Office said they pulled more than 200 servers offline and estimated that about 1,800 paying customers used Kratos to run roughly 15,000 phishing campaigns a month.
  • Kratos was designed to steal Microsoft 365 session cookies as well as passwords, allowing attackers to bypass two-factor authentication and access accounts as the user.
  • ANY.RUN found that Kratos offered a plain PHP credential-harvesting mode and a Node.js reverse-proxy mode that relayed logins to Microsoft in real time and captured the resulting session.
  • Authorities said victims since late 2024 number in the hundreds of thousands across more than 30 countries, with concentrations in Europe and the United States.

Chick-fil-A discloses data breach after credential stuffing attacks — Should Read

Chick-fil-A is notifying customers after attackers used stolen third-party credentials in a June credential stuffing campaign to access some Chick-fil-A One accounts. Exposed data may include names, emails, membership/payment identifiers, rewards balances, partial card numbers, and stored contact details, prompting the company to log out affected users, remove payment methods, restore balances, and urge password changes.

  • Chick-fil-A is notifying an undisclosed number of customers after suspicious login activity led it to discover that some Chick-fil-A One accounts had been hacked.
  • The company said unauthorized parties used credentials obtained from a third-party source in an automated attack against its website and mobile application between June 17 and June 19, 2026.
  • Information potentially accessed includes customers’ names, email addresses, Chick-fil-A One membership numbers, mobile pay numbers, QR codes, Chick-fil-A credit amounts, the last four digits of credit or debit card numbers, and, if stored, birth dates, phone numbers, and addresses.
  • Chick-fil-A told the Texas Attorney General that the breach impacts 2,182 Texans and also sent notification letters to residents of several other U.S. states and the District of Columbia.
  • In response, Chick-fil-A logged out impacted accounts, removed payment methods, restored Chick-fil-A One account balances, added rewards to affected accounts, and advised users to change their passwords.

Trojanized Newtonsoft.Json Fork Hides Game-Rigging Code in a Working Library — Should Read

A typosquatted NuGet package posing as Newtonsoft.Json was a working trojanized fork designed to manipulate Digitain crash-game results and later exfiltrate rigged outcomes to an attacker-controlled server. The malware only activates in Digitain’s specific backend context, making it difficult for other developers who installed it to notice anything wrong.

  • Cybersecurity researchers discovered a NuGet typosquat named Newtonsoftt.Json.Net that masquerades as the Newtonsoft.Json library and contains code designed to rig live game results on Digitain.
  • Seven versions of Newtonsoftt.Json.Net were published to NuGet by the owner MagicalPuff96, and the package has been downloaded about 1,200 times.
  • JFrog said the trojanized library activates after JsonConvert.DefaultSettings is initialized and targets servers running Digitain’s FG-Crash crash-game backend.
  • Later versions of the package exfiltrate rigged round results to an attacker-controlled server at 185.126.237[.]64:5341 using the header X-Seq-ApiKey: theperfectheist2025.
  • Developers are advised to remove the typosquat package, block the command-and-control address, and pin Newtonsoft.Json to a known-good version via packages.lock.json.

Agentic SOC Autonomy: Earn It One Decision at a Time — Optional

AI agents in the SOC should earn autonomy gradually, starting with low-risk tasks like enrichment and only moving to automated remediation after their decisions are measurable, auditable, and reversible. The key is to grant trust one decision class at a time, with clear outcome metrics and rollback plans before any agent is allowed to act on its own.

  • The article argues that autonomy in a security operations center is not a feature to switch on, but a level of trust an AI agent must earn one decision class at a time.
  • The author distinguishes between agents that recommend actions and agents that take actions, noting that bad automated remediation can disrupt business operations and damage trust in the security team.
  • The article recommends separating agent work into detection, enrichment, correlation, recommendation, and action, then granting trust to each stage independently.
  • The author says every agent decision should be logged, attributable, and reconstructable so teams can explain why the agent acted during a post-incident review.
  • The article states that automated remediation should not be enabled unless there is a tested, fast, and well-understood rollback plan for when the agent is wrong.

UK Cybercrime Journal: H1 2026 Dark Web Seizures & Arrests — Optional

UK and European law enforcement disrupted several dark web criminal operations in early 2026, including drug markets and a bogus murder-for-hire site, through arrests, infrastructure seizures, and cryptocurrency recovery. The key takeaway is that while Tor, Telegram, and crypto enable these markets, investigators can still contain them by infiltrating platforms, tracing payments, and identifying operators.

  • On 14 May 2026, two Cambridgeshire drug dealers were sentenced after ERSOU arrested them in July 2024 for using the dark web to supply heroin, cocaine, and amphetamine to hundreds of users across the UK.
  • The Gorgonites operation used a Telegram channel to arrange drug deals and was linked to at least 570 individual sales on Nemesis Market since September 2023.
  • On 17 March 2026, the London Metropolitan Police’s Cyber Crime Unit announced the seizure of AEGIS Marketplace, which had 30 active sellers and an estimated 10,000 drug sales in ten months.
  • On 19 January 2026, two suspects were arrested in Romania as part of an ERSOU investigation into Online Killers Marketplace, a bogus dark web site offering services including murder and extortion.
  • The Online Killers Marketplace investigation led to the seizure of at least $600,000 in cryptocurrency, almost €50,000 in cash, and around £48,000 worth of Romanian Leu.
